vignette: Arthur Vance was fifty when he finally sat across from a clinician, but the work began years earlier. He was forty-eight the night he went to a downtown hotel bar to meet a former graduate student. He expected a quiet conversation about practice management. Instead, the room tilted. The air grew thick with the sharp, sour tang of spilled bourbon and vodka. He tried to stand, but his limbs refused to obey. He was trapped in the heavy upholstered chair, aware of every second passing in paralyzed silence. When two emergency vehicles pulled up outside, the wail of their sirens cut through the lobby glass. The sound did not bring rescue; it only mirrored the helplessness he was feeling. He felt completely uncomfortable, a raw, crawling awareness of his own powerlessness that settled deep into his bones. When Arthur returned to his private psychology practice, he told himself he could compartmentalize. He continued to see clients, but his own internal landscape began to shift. In his office, he sometimes attempted to reconstruct the night to understand what had gone wrong. He would begin to trace the sequence of events, only to find himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it. He explained this to his supervisor during one of his required peer consultations, noting that he couldn't seem to put the frightening event into words. The experience lived in him as a somatic voltage rather than a narrative. Some evenings, he would wake at exactly 2 a.m., his heart hammering against his ribs, feeling the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory. He did not know what had been done to him, only that he was carrying a terror that refused to name itself. Arthur adjusted his environment. He stopped accepting referral cases involving substance-induced crises or sexual trauma. He altered his morning drive to the clinic, taking perimeter roads to avoid the intersection where he frequently encountered emergency traffic. When he heard sirens, his jaw would tighten, and he would grip the steering wheel until his knuckles blanched, forcing his breathing to stay even. He began carrying unscented hand sanitizer and mints, constantly aware of any lingering smell of alcohol on his own clothes or in a colleague's office. The adjustments persisted. Over nearly two years, the routines solidified. He could no longer sit in a dimly lit conference room without tracking the exits. His wife, Elena, noticed the quiet withdrawal. They stopped cooking dinner together. He was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him-holding space for a colleague's burnout with steady empathy, or allowing himself to rest without a pulse of anticipation. He felt dead inside, watching his own days pass like unread files. Sometimes, when Elena rested her hand on his shoulder, he stiffened, certain that he was an object, not like a person, but something handled and set down. Arthur came to his current provider's office because his insurance auditors flagged his recent session notes as incomplete, and because the hollow routine had begun to interfere with his clinical judgment. He sat on the edge of the couch, his posture rigid, waiting for the therapist to speak. He was most afraid of what might surface if he stopped pushing, but he was hoping, with a quiet exhaustion, that someone could help him feel solid again.
